subject: geography
title: US Middle School Geography - Population and Migration Readings
subtitle: Reading passages on density, migration, urbanisation, case studies, and displacement
description: Source-faithful reading comprehension passages for a human geography unit on population and migration.

data.sourcePassage: People are not spread evenly across Earth. Many high-population areas are near coasts, rivers, fertile plains, transport routes, jobs, schools, hospitals, and safer political conditions. Areas with extreme cold or heat, dry deserts, steep mountains, dense forests, poor soils, or limited services often have lower population density. Density matters because two places can have the same total population but very different pressure on land, housing, transport, schools, parks, waste systems, and emergency services. High density can support public transport and nearby services, but it can also create congestion, expensive housing, and pressure on water or sanitation systems.

questions.question: Which places often support higher population concentrations?
questions.modelAnswer: Coasts, rivers, and fertile plains often support higher population concentrations.

questions.question: What does population density compare?
questions.modelAnswer: Population density compares the number of people with the amount of land area.

questions.question: Explain why two places with the same population can feel very different.
questions.modelAnswer: They can have different land areas. If one place has the same population on less land, it has higher density and may feel more crowded.

questions.question: Give one benefit and one challenge of high population density.
questions.modelAnswer: A benefit is that public transport and services can reach many people. A challenge is pressure on housing, traffic, water, or sanitation.

questions.question: Why should geographers avoid saying that high density is always bad?
questions.modelAnswer: High density can create challenges, but it can also support efficient transport, nearby services, cultural diversity, and less land used per person.

data.sourceTitle: Push and Pull Factors in Migration
data.targetTitle: Push and Pull Factors in Migration
data.sourcePassage: Migration decisions are often shaped by push and pull factors. Push factors encourage or force people to leave a place. They include few jobs, low wages, conflict, unsafe conditions, drought, crop failure, natural disasters, discrimination, persecution, and poor access to education or health care. Pull factors attract people to another place. They include job opportunities, higher wages, safety, schools, family connections, health care, political freedom, and reliable water or food supply. Migration is rarely caused by only one factor. A family may move because drought has hurt farming, relatives already live in a city, and the city offers more work.
data.targetPassage: Migration decisions are often shaped by push and pull factors. Push factors encourage or force people to leave a place. They include few jobs, low wages, conflict, unsafe conditions, drought, crop failure, natural disasters, discrimination, persecution, and poor access to education or health care. Pull factors attract people to another place. They include job opportunities, higher wages, safety, schools, family connections, health care, political freedom, and reliable water or food supply. Migration is rarely caused by only one factor. A family may move because drought has hurt farming, relatives already live in a city, and the city offers more work.

questions.question: Which option is a push factor?
questions.modelAnswer: Conflict in the home region is a push factor because it encourages people to leave.

questions.question: Which option is a pull factor?
questions.modelAnswer: Job opportunities are a pull factor because they attract people to a destination.

questions.question: Why is migration rarely explained by only one cause?
questions.modelAnswer: People often respond to several linked pressures and opportunities, such as jobs, family, drought, education, safety, and health care.

questions.question: How could drought be connected to both environmental and economic migration?
questions.modelAnswer: Drought is environmental because it reduces water and crops. It can become economic when farmers lose income and seek work elsewhere.

questions.question: Explain why people with family networks may have more migration options.
questions.modelAnswer: Family networks can provide information, housing, money, language help, childcare, or job contacts, making movement less risky.

data.sourcePassage: Urbanisation means that a larger share of people live in urban areas. It can happen when people move from rural areas to cities, when cities grow outward, when towns become larger and more urban, or when births in cities are higher than deaths. Urbanisation can create opportunities, including more jobs, universities, hospitals, cultural exchange, public transport, and services. It can also create challenges, including housing shortages, informal settlements in some regions, traffic, air pollution, waste problems, and pressure on water and electricity systems. Sustainable planning tries to manage growth so people have housing, transport, services, and environmental protection.

questions.question: What does urbanisation mean?
options: A larger share of people live in urban areas
questions.modelAnswer: Urbanisation means a larger share of people live in urban areas.

questions.question: Which is named as a challenge of urbanisation?
options: Too much empty farmland inside every city
questions.modelAnswer: Housing shortages are one challenge of urbanisation.

questions.question: Explain one way urbanisation can create opportunities.
questions.modelAnswer: Urbanisation can create opportunities by concentrating jobs, schools, hospitals, markets, transport, and cultural activities in one place.

questions.question: Why might city leaders need to plan transport during rapid growth?
questions.modelAnswer: More residents need to travel to jobs, schools, shops, and services, so roads, buses, rail, and walking routes may face pressure.

questions.question: What would make urban growth more sustainable?
questions.modelAnswer: Sustainable growth would include affordable housing, clean transport, safe water, waste management, green space, and protection from hazards.

data.sourcePassage: Egypt shows why population distribution is not explained by land area alone. Egypt is mostly desert, but many people live along the Nile River and in the Nile Delta. The Nile provides water for farming, daily life, transport, cities, and trade. Fertile soil near the river helps crops grow, while the surrounding desert has much lower settlement density. This pattern creates benefits and challenges. The river supports large populations and economic activity, but high density near the Nile can put pressure on housing, water quality, farmland, and city services. Climate change and upstream water use may also create water management issues.

questions.question: Where is much of Egypt's population concentrated?
options: Along the Nile River and Nile Delta
Only in the far Sahara interior
questions.modelAnswer: Much of Egypt's population is concentrated along the Nile River and Nile Delta.

questions.question: Which resource does the Nile provide?
options: Water for farming and daily life
questions.modelAnswer: The Nile provides water for farming and daily life.

questions.question: Explain why land area alone does not explain Egypt's population pattern.
questions.modelAnswer: Egypt has a large land area, but much is desert. People cluster near the Nile because it provides water, fertile soil, transport, and jobs.

questions.question: Give one challenge caused by high density near the Nile.
questions.modelAnswer: High density near the Nile can pressure housing, water quality, farmland, city services, or water management.

questions.question: How does the Egypt example connect physical and human geography?
questions.modelAnswer: The physical river and desert shape settlement, while farming, trade, cities, housing, and water management show human decisions and impacts.

data.sourcePassage: Migration can be voluntary or forced, and the difference is sometimes complicated. Voluntary migration happens when people choose to move, such as moving for college, work, family, or lifestyle. Forced migration happens when danger or extreme pressure pushes people from their homes. Examples include war, persecution, severe flooding, wildfire, famine, and forced removal. Refugees leave their country because of danger or persecution, while internally displaced people leave home but remain inside their own country. Displaced people may need safety, shelter, food, clean water, medical care, education, legal protection, and connection with family. Host communities may gain new workers, businesses, and cultural exchange, while also needing more school places, housing, services, and international support.

questions.question: Which situation is an example of forced migration?
options: Leaving because war makes home unsafe
Choosing a holiday by the sea
Moving bedroom inside the same house
questions.modelAnswer: Leaving because war makes home unsafe is forced migration.

questions.question: What is the difference between a refugee and an internally displaced person?
options: A refugee crosses a country border; an internally displaced person remains inside their country
A refugee always moves for college
An internally displaced person is never forced to move
questions.modelAnswer: A refugee crosses a country border, while an internally displaced person remains inside their country.

questions.question: Name three needs displaced people may have after leaving home.
questions.modelAnswer: They may need safety, shelter, food, clean water, medical care, education, legal protection, and family connection.

questions.question: How can forced migration affect host communities?
questions.modelAnswer: Host communities may gain workers, businesses, and cultural exchange, but may also need more housing, schools, services, and support.

questions.question: Why can the line between voluntary and forced migration be complicated?
questions.modelAnswer: People may choose to move, but their choices can be strongly limited by drought, unsafe conditions, poverty, disasters, or lack of services.
